name: Tianzhao Mandate
summary: An ancient bureaucratic empire built on the assumption that reality has structure, where a strange problem isn't natural or supernatural, just a question of which office is responsible for it.
government: The Bearer of the Mandate rules from the Celestial Throne through an enormous examined civil service of ministries, records and provincial offices, including a Ministry of Ritual & Anomalous Affairs.
knownFor: Its bureaucracy and examinations, tea, paper seals and notices, the Registry of Recognized Powers, and politely doing nothing until you give up.
gateAttitude: Tianzhao first interpreted the Gates through its existing concepts of the Spirit and Celestial realms.
beliefs:
There's no single church. Religious life is an overlapping mix of **Heaven**, the **ancestors**, local gods, spirits, household rites, the **courts of the dead** and reincarnation, and someone can honour their ancestors in the morning, petition the city god at noon and call a spirit specialist when the house makes noises at night without seeing any contradiction. None of it has ever produced an effect a foreign scholar could measure; before the Gates the world had no magic at all, and Tianzhao simply had the most thorough administration for the possibility.

**Heaven** is order itself, not necessarily a god with a face. Popular cosmology has **Three Realms**, Mortal, Spirit and Celestial, with permeable borders. The supernatural is imagined as a **celestial bureaucracy**: powers responsible for rivers, cities, roads, harvests and death. Five well-loved figures: the **Jade Chancellor** of divine law and records (immensely powerful, and still not Heaven: even the highest office is an office); **Lady Shun**, Keeper of Names, for ancestry and the records of the dead; **General Bao**, Lord of the Red Gate, guardian of thresholds and now hugely popular with Expeditioners (nothing suggests he has anything to do with the Gates themselves); **Mistress Lin** of Ten Thousand Remedies, patron of physicians; and the **Laughing Magistrate**, whose stories are about rigid procedure losing to common sense.

The dead are guided by the **Collectors**, or Officers of Passage, in official hats with registers and lanterns, often irritated by paperwork. Ghosts are a failure of proper passage. The state's **Registry of Recognized Powers** can give a river spirit a title and a temple, and a god who keeps failing in their duties can face petitions and review. A village once asked for a review of its river lord's title *"or, failing that, assistance with the bridge."* Talismans read less like spells than notices: *you do not have permission to enter*. People are careful about giving their full name to unknown beings, and researchers now apply the same caution beyond the Gates.

One old tale, **the Painted Door**, about a scholar who steps into a painted palace and comes back decades later, has become newly interesting; some researchers wonder whether it remembers something Gate-like, and nothing has been confirmed. The most repeated story of the Gate era says a Collector stopped at a Gate threshold and said: *"Beyond this door, your name is not in my register."* It's unauthenticated, disputed and everywhere, and any Pavilion scholar will ask you who exactly witnessed it.
history:
The ruler governs through the **Mandate of Heaven**, which isn't guaranteed by blood. It depends on keeping proper relationship between the people, the state, the land, the ancestors and the greater order, and a dynasty can hold it legitimately and later lose it. So Tianzhao reads its history as **dynastic cycles**: a dynasty restores order, builds institutions, grows rigid or corrupt, and is replaced. Every official learns the pattern as a warning. Rebels don't take the Mandate; rebels are what you see once it has already been lost, usually after somebody stopped writing down that the granaries were short. The Archive doesn't hold a full record of the dynasties.

The state runs on an enormous examined bureaucracy. Some ministries would be familiar anywhere (Grain, Waters, Roads and Works, War); others puzzle foreigners: **Heavenly Observation** watches the sky and the calendar, and **Ritual & Anomalous Affairs** handles reported spirits, hauntings and the beings the state recognises. A flood can be engineering, agriculture, law and a river spirit at once, and the instinct is to route it to all the right offices. The engineer asked whether his embankment failure is engineering, agricultural, legal or divine answers *"Yes"*, and the clerk reaches for four more forms.

For long stretches, the **Closed Centuries**, Tianzhao restricted foreign access to designated ports and formal channels, and its politics still prefer restraint: delayed approvals, revoked permits, changes in ceremonial precedence and privileges quietly allowed to expire. A Tianzhao official can destroy a diplomat's position without raising their voice. **Tea** has been grown here for centuries, and when Aurelia adopted it as a national habit, one diplomat summed up the view: *"If they insist upon measuring civilisation in leaves, be grateful the leaves grow here."* Tariffs and shipping rights on tea are real leverage. Older officials still call Vesper by its royal name, **Solenne**, which may be bureaucratic habit, a very subtle insult, or both.

**The Gates.** The first explanation was that they might lead into the Spirit Realm, but the evidence didn't fit cleanly: specialists report some spirits perceive Gates while others refuse to approach them. Four theories compete: **Distant Provinces** of the same order, **Outer Spirit Realms**, **Foreign Heavens** with their own order, and the uncomfortable, unofficial **Heavenless Places**. In Endros the Mandate keeps the **Pavilion of Celestial Affairs**: embassy, research institute, temple, observatory and archive, gardened and closely administered, where visitors are received with perfect courtesy and rarely see more than they were meant to.
visualSummary:
Tianzhao looks like a very old civilisation that took in railways and factories without deciding its past needed replacing. The palette is **cinnabar red, jade green, ink black, ivory, muted gold and deep blue**, with clouds, cranes and gates as motifs. In the cities, courtyards and walled compounds stand beside railways and chimneys, the new buildings fitted into the old rooflines.

Dress means layered robes, structured coats, broad sleeves, high collars and **rank badges**, with field and factory clothes adapting the old forms rather than dropping them. Paper is everywhere, and official notices, ritual inscriptions, permits and containment warnings often look alike, because they often are alike. Ask whether the strip of red paper on a crate is a spell and you'll be told *"No. It is a notice,"* and then, as your hand reaches the lid, *"You should still not remove it."* Machinery is precise and symmetrical, with ceramic parts and lacquered surfaces. Factories keep a shrine next to the safety placard and geomancers work beside engineers: as one press operator put it, the guard rails make the press safe, and the shrine makes sure everyone remembers it can kill you.

The admired person observes before acting, considers consequences and prefers the correct result to the dramatic gesture. Avoidable heroic sacrifice tends to be seen as poor planning. Foreigners decide Tianzhao is mystical, stagnant or inscrutable. It's none of those: its people aren't speaking in riddles, they're being polite, its technology is modern, and very little is truly hidden. It's just filed under a category the visitor didn't think to ask about.

relations.text: A polite rivalry over ports, access and influence; tea is leverage.
An old trading partner that accepts Tianzhao's restrictions while the trade stays worthwhile.
Mutual respect for craft; disagreement over metaphysical caution.
Admires its science, not its constant agitation; older officials still say 'Solenne'.
Strong scholarly respect; Verna wants Tianzhao's archives, and access is granted sparingly.
